turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Monday, the ninth of November. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three up top. Nine dead across two Polish towns — and a terrorism label applied inside a day. [pause] We'll show you why we're holding it loosely.
An auction house in Geneva closes a record sale and publishes no total — so this desk did the addition itself.
And later, the sport where the grade with the most accidents is the easy one. [deadpan] Ice climbing.
[curious] The easy one is the one that hurts people?
That's the one. Hold the thought. Start in Kraków.
Saturday afternoon. A twenty-four-year-old Polish man, Michał O., fired from a car into the streets around Kraków's main market square. Six killed.
[exhales] In the square itself?

The streets around it. Then, a hundred and fifty kilometres north-east, in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, three more bodies at his family home — believed to be his parents and his sister. Nine dead across the two towns. Sixteen wounded. Two officers critically hurt.
Did he hold a licence?
A valid firearms permit. And a shooting club in Starachowice said publicly that he had never trained there in dynamic, tactical or combat shooting.
And the motive?

Prosecutors have opened a terrorism investigation — the evidence, they say, indicates the same person committed the acts in both cities. The interior minister said early findings indicated, quote, very radical far-right views, while cautioning it's unconfirmed and the motive unknown. Tusk declared two days of mourning, and Saint Mary's hourly trumpet call was silent for twelve hours.
[exhales] Twelve hours of no trumpet. That's the sound of a city stopping.

Now the sceptic box. The label was applied inside a day, before anybody had spoken to the suspect — he's critical, and not formally detained. No manifesto, no claim, no network reported. And three family members killed at home, then strangers in public, is also the signature of a familicide.
[pause] So nobody can tell you which it is yet.
Nobody can. We're printing both.
Jerusalem. Five o'clock Sunday afternoon: President Isaac Herzog formally tasked Gadi Eisenkot with forming Israel's next government. Twenty-eight days, extendable by fourteen.
[curious] He won the recommendations and lost the election?

Both. Sixty-seven recommendations against Netanyahu's forty-six — and yet his four parties hold forty-eight seats to Netanyahu's fifty-three. Arab-led parties won a record nineteen, and nineteen of his recommendations are theirs. Liberman's party won't sit with them.
So what's the other door?

Forty-eight, plus United Torah Judaism's seven, plus Shas's six. Sixty-one — a majority by a seat. But Shas called cooperation reports, quote, total fake news, and a Shas source added: there is no scenario in which Shas rabbis will act against United Torah Judaism rabbis.
[skeptical] So the clock runs on a shut door.

And one small thing that sits right on our spine. Turkey's Official Gazette has now passed a fourth day — the sixth to the ninth of November — without publishing the Mecca pact, which parliament ratified two hundred and seventy-nine to a hundred and nineteen.
And nothing is in force until it's printed.
By the pact's own second article. The clock hasn't started, and nobody has said why.
The money desk. Brent crude fell about twelve and a half per cent in the week to Friday the sixth.
Somebody opened a tap?
Nobody opened anything. Diplomacy between Washington and Tehran, mediated by Qatar, took the war premium out of a barrel without adding a single barrel.
[amused] So the price fell on a conversation.

Precisely. Now the part worth your attention. The nominal American ten-year fell from four point nine one to four point eight six per cent. The real ten-year rose — two point six two, to two point six three.
Wait. The nominal fell and the real went up?

The inflation compensation between them went from two point two nine to two point two three. The entire rally was those six basis points. The bond market didn't change its mind about growth. It changed its mind about oil.
And the jobs number?

Payrolls a hundred and sixty-five thousand, unemployment four point one per cent. The two-year fell to four point four six on Thursday's rout and came back to four point five one. Call it a deflating supply-shock scare with a hawkish central bank attached.
Did the balanced portfolio do its job?

It did. Nasdaq down five and a half per cent Thursday, the S and P down four point four, bonds rallied. But read the invoice: the cushion came from breakevens, not real yields. Paid for by the oil price, not by the bond market's view of growth.
[thoughtful] Lucky, not clever.

And bitcoin fell two point six per cent, then flat-lined all weekend inside a five hundred and sixty-five dollar band. In a week when the haven trade paid four per cent, bitcoin lost two and a half. Explanation, not advice.
And us?
Shut for Deepavali observed, so Friday's close stands. The Straits Times fell two point two one per cent — a timing artefact. We closed before Wall Street bounced.

Singapore proper. The Land Transport Authority told reporters on the sixth that Grab must stop testing autonomous vehicles at junctions like the one in Punggol, where a driverless shuttle came close to a schoolgirl at eleven minutes past eight on the fifth.
[curious] Walk me through it. Properly.

The authority's own data account, in order. The vehicle detected two pedestrians and tracked them. They stood still. Its light turned green and it began a left turn. When the girl started to cross — her signal green, but blinking — it braked and veered right. Then the operator took manual control and steered away.
And nobody was hit.
Nobody was hit. But it's the first time a Singapore regulator has halted any part of the programme since public shuttles began on the first of April. Grab's line: safety is our top priority.
Naturally.

The clip went up on Facebook, posted by S G Road Vigilante. Both outlets that reported it describe a split audience — some blamed the girl, some thought the vehicle reacted too slowly. One said it was the talk of many Punggol chats, with parents asking who's responsible.
And that question has no published answer.

None. Two more. Indonesia's social affairs ministry has declared eighteen adoptions in Singapore illegal, after a Bandung court sentenced thirteen people for falsifying residency papers — each child reportedly sold for about three hundred million rupiah. No Singapore reply at all. And it's day three, and neither M one nor Doctor Anywhere has said how many customers its breach exposed. M one's release names the data taken, but no regulator — only, quote, the relevant authorities.
[wry] The relevant authorities.
Another number nobody published.

Technology. Commerce extended its Affiliates Rule stay to the tenth of January, twenty twenty-seven — published on the ninth, the morning the rule was due to bite, and giving no reason at all. The rule extends export restrictions automatically to any firm half-owned or more by a listed party.
And there's a correction here, I think.
Ours, and it belongs on that page. Yesterday's issue recorded the rule as returning with nothing filed. The stay had in fact been released on the fifth. Sixty-two days bought.
[warmly] Good. Say it out loud.

Also: roughly six hundred thousand Nvidia H two hundreds are reported sitting in Hong Kong warehouses, because China hasn't approved large-volume imports. And a Commerce official told a House hearing that no such sale has been approved at all.
So the chips are warehoused for a sale that doesn't exist.

The two accounts cannot both be whole, and we can't say which breaks. The home lab, meanwhile: Raspberry Pi raised its sixteen-gigabyte Model Five by eighty dollars, to three hundred and eighty-five, blaming a lack of alternative supply. The post doesn't print the old price — three hundred and eighty-five less eighty is three hundred and five, so a rise of twenty-six point two per cent. That's our arithmetic, not a published figure.
[wry] Spine of the week. Sixth time on that blog, isn't it?

Sixth memory-driven price move in twelve months. Hacker News gave it three points and two comments. And the Kit: Apple's top sixteen-inch MacBook Pro now configures to fourteen thousand five hundred and forty-nine dollars — but nobody buys the sixteen-terabyte drive that adds seven thousand of it. The honest datapoint is the base fourteen-inch, going from one thousand six hundred and ninety-nine to one thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine.
On the machine people actually buy. That's the real one.

The Atelier: pencils. And almost every good pencil in the world comes from the same tree and the same mill — incense cedar from California and Oregon, sawn by one American family firm, in a factory it owns in Tianjin, China.
One mill. For everybody.

Broadly. And here's the part that should annoy you. The grading scale is not standardised. No universal graphite-to-clay ratio sits behind the letters — H B is a house opinion, and a Japanese H B lays down about a grade darker than a German one.
Wait — really? [laughs] So the whole alphabet is vibes.

The whole alphabet is vibes. And a pencil stops getting better at Mitsubishi's Hi-Uni and Tombow's MONO one hundred — twenty dollars a dozen, one dollar sixty-seven each. Blackwing is thirty-four: a Japanese pencil in a Californian wrapper with a dead American name, and Pencil Talk called the original Eberhard Faber six-oh-two average in darkness and smoothness.
[laughs] Okay, that's brutal.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Must you.
Every single time. Ice climbing, Claire. Go.
Start with the recalls, because they set the tone. Petzl recalled five thousand three hundred and sixty Nomic and Ergonomic axes in March, after twenty-six shafts broke at the handle.
[exhales] At the handle. The bit you hang from.
C point A point M point P recalled two thousand two hundred and thirty more on the fifth of November — three days before this issue. Nobody was hurt in either.
Right. Teach me the grades.
Water ice one needs no axes at all. Water ice three is sustained seventy degrees. Water ice five is a full pitch of near-vertical. And water ice seven — Will Gadd calls that one semi-mythical.
[laughs] Semi-mythical. I love that.
And the grade with the most accidents is water ice two.
[skeptical] The easy one?
The easy one. Where people stop being careful.
[pause] That's genuinely chilling. And obvious the moment you say it.
It's the whole sport in one line. At the other end — Helmcken Falls, routes graded water ice ten to water ice thirteen, bolted since twenty ten. The ceiling hasn't moved since twenty twenty.
Nobody's gone harder since.
Nobody published going harder. And here's a lovely hole in the record: nobody knows how many ice climbers there are. The industry doesn't count them separately.
Of course it doesn't.
The friendliest door in is the Ouray Ice Park — over a hundred and fifty named routes across nearly two miles of gorge. Free, public, and farmed by a nonprofit that sprays water down the walls.
[excited] Hang on — they farm the ice?
They farm the ice. And demand isn't the problem: at the Bozeman Ice Festival in December, almost all of some twenty-five clinics have sold out.
So people want in. What does the gear cost?

A Black Diamond Hydra is three hundred and ninety-nine ninety-five. A Petzl Nomic, three hundred and seventy-nine ninety-five. Grivel's rebranded Nexus Machine, a reported seven hundred and fifty-nine. A tool.
Each. Not a pair.
Each. And my favourite line in the whole feature: a pair of Petzl Dart forefoot sections — a spare part — is two hundred and thirty-nine ninety-five Canadian. Dearer than many whole crampons.
[laughs] A spare part? That's absurd.
Does the marketing at least behave?

[deadpan] It does not. On Edelrid's lightest ice screw, Torstein Derauf did the arithmetic: the blue is two grams lighter than a rival, and the red isn't lighter at all. He called it mildly deceitful marketing. Kevin Mcbride, who's actually used them, wrote: my advice to anyone looking at buying these is simple. Don't.
That is a review.

The economics are tidier than you'd expect, though. A complete buy-once outfit is roughly two thousand nine hundred to three thousand three hundred dollars — and the whole ceiling of the sport's gear economy is about five thousand.

Now the serious part. A peer-reviewed study puts one New Hampshire valley's season at ninety-nine days now — and thirty by twenty one hundred, on the highest emissions path. And in January of this year the Ouray Ice Park could not open. It opened two days before its own festival.
[thoughtful] Two days. After they'd sold the tickets.
Joseph W. Dutton put it bluntly. Global warming has wrecked this sport.
Is that the consensus?
No. Double J called it the worst season he could remember in Utah — while Nick Huhn said, quote, here in the Midwest it has been great.
So the season didn't shrink.
It moved. That's the honest version.

Screen and Sound. Godzilla Minus Zero opened to thirty-one million six hundred and ten thousand dollars in North America, from three thousand two hundred and fifty-four cinemas — the American number one, and a company record for GKIDS, whose previous best was thirteen million.
[excited] A Japanese monster film, top of the American chart.

Second-biggest opening ever for a live-action film not in English in America, behind The Passion of the Christ. But it fell thirty-five per cent Friday to Saturday — a front-loaded fanbase curve, not legs. And Japan's own opening-weekend figure does not exist at source.
[laughs] There it is again.
There it is again — and it brings us to the cover. Phillips closed its Geneva Watch Auction twenty-four on Sunday afternoon, and published no total.
So you added it up.

We downloaded all two hundred and twenty-five lot entries, parsed them, and added the two hundred and eleven published results. [pause] Ninety-one million nine hundred and twenty-two thousand two hundred and fifty Swiss francs.
[excited] That's a number nobody else has.

It's a floor, not a total — ten lots carry no published result, so the sell-through cannot be stated. On that floor it beats the seventy-four point eight million of the May sale by about twenty-three per cent.
And the headline lot?

A titanium F point P point Journe Résonance, made for the Tokyo boutique. Estimated at four hundred to eight hundred thousand. Sold for six million one hundred and forty-six thousand — seven point seven times its high estimate.
[drawn out] What? Okay, that's absurd.

And the sceptic box earns its keep: a record built on lots selling at seven times their ceiling is a record about the estimates. The cover itself is a Cartier Portico mystery clock, lot two hundred and twenty, sold on the eighth for four million eight hundred and fifteen thousand Swiss francs — and it did not beat its own estimate.
On the cover of a record sale.

And Audio-Technica's three thousand seven hundred and ninety-nine dollar headphone, in Kiso hinoki with Echizen urushi lacquer, met listeners at the forty-second Autumn Headphone Festival. Still no published measurement, four issues after we asked.
[sighs] Beautiful wood, though.

The family desk. The World Health Organization reported on the fourth that a quarter of the world's adolescents — about two hundred and forty million — could not name a single day in the previous week with an hour of activity. Three hundred and eighty-nine surveys, a hundred and forty countries, more than three point two million people aged eleven to seventeen.
[exhales] Not one day. Is this the screens story?

That's the instinct, and the data refuses it. It has barely moved in fifteen years. The mean is two point seven active days, and twenty-eight per cent of girls report zero against twenty-two per cent of boys. And this desk could not obtain a single confidence interval.
If devices had collapsed how much children move, that's the series where it would show.

And it doesn't. Better news from France, though. A trial moved school from eight o'clock to nine for four classes and measured six months of sleep. They gained twenty-two point eight minutes a night, and bedtimes did not drift later to swallow it — the shift was eight point nine minutes earlier, and not significant.
[excited] So they kept it. And the catch?
They randomised four classes and analysed about fifty individuals as though independent — they say so themselves. So those confidence intervals are almost certainly too narrow.

Fitness. A randomised trial in Porto Alegre found that gripping something hard for two minutes at a time, three times a week, lowered daytime blood pressure in adults already medicated for it — awake diastolic down about four and a half millimetres of mercury. The identical protocol done with the far larger muscles of the thigh moved nothing at all.
[skeptical] The bigger muscles did nothing?

Nothing. The response, the authors conclude, is not determined solely by the amount of muscle mass recruited. But pressure over twenty-four hours was recorded once, after the intervention, with no baseline — and it ran at half the evidence-based duration. General guidance, not medical advice.

Travel. Singapore Airlines showed its twenty twenty-seven cabins on the sixth: the business seat is twenty-two inches wide on the A three fifty, against twenty-eight on the seat it replaces. More seats, more screen, less shoulder.
[exhales] A six-inch cut. And the reviewers led on that?

They led on the colour. Rhys Jones called it virtually unrecognisable as a Singapore Airlines seat. The grand tour is Rajasthan — Jaipur averages twenty-nine point six degrees and one point nine millimetres of rain in November, against forty-one point one in May, and the Pushkar camel fair runs the seventeenth to the twenty-fourth.
And the air, since that's the usual objection?

Our correction: Jaipur ran at roughly half Delhi's index on the day we checked, but its bad-air episodes are longer and more persistent. And Jantar Mantar's great sundial is ruled at two-second intervals — while the standard reference site says the shadow's own edge may span six to seven of those marks.
Twelve to fourteen seconds of blur on a scale ruled at two.

Precision you cannot read. The diary: Kabukiza puts December's tickets on sale at ten o'clock on the fourteenth of November — the only row in the agenda whose window opens after this issue. Four thousand five hundred to seventeen thousand yen, and anyone aged thirty or under gets a half-price same-day seat.
[warmly] That is a lovely rule.
And the sceptic on the table: of the first eight restaurants we checked, four weren't new at all. One had opened in February, twenty twenty-five.
[laughs] New.
[pause] The Undercurrent. Slow down for this one.
China's animation flood.

In the first half of this year, Chinese studios released two hundred and twenty-one thousand nine hundred new animated serials onto a single app. More than twelve hundred episodes a day. At the peak, one new title roughly every thirty-six seconds. Almost all of it made by artificial intelligence.
[drawn out] Every thirty-six seconds.

For scale: the whole country produced thirty-three thousand live-action micro-dramas in all of twenty twenty-five. The form is called manju — literally comic-drama, glossed as a visualised novel. A hundred-minute title costs about a hundred and ten thousand yuan instead of four to five hundred thousand, and takes seven to fifteen days instead of twenty-five to forty.
[thoughtful] That's a real productivity gain. So who got the money?
Not the producers. Revenue per ten thousand plays fell from thirty to a hundred yuan — down to five to ten. One practitioner's eleven series, sixteen episodes each, earned nine yuan sixty in total.
[pause] Nine yuan sixty.

Now the mechanism — the whole issue in one paragraph. ByteDance's app pays creators by total watch time, times unit price, times a coefficient. Neither the unit price nor the coefficient is published. A producer named Yuan Min told a Shanghai newspaper that after a coefficient change, a title he expected to bring in over a million yuan came in at a hundred to two hundred thousand.
[scoffs] And every other link in that chain —

— belongs to the same company. The web fiction. The video model, billed per second. The traffic, which is seventy per cent of a producer's cost. And the money coming back, under a formula ByteDance writes. When the model upgraded, the price per second went up.
Of course it did.

So the argument is simple. The productivity gain never reaches the producer — it passes straight through to whoever controls distribution. And the regulator gave us a number by accident: filing thresholds for AI micro-dramas set at eight hundred thousand and three hundred thousand yuan, against live-action's three million and one million. About thirty per cent.
[thoughtful] So the state wrote down a seventy per cent cost deflation —

— without anybody having to estimate it. There is a counter-case, though. The app's daily users rose a hundred and seven per cent, to a hundred and sixty-eight million, the analyst has the market growing a hundred and thirty-eight per cent, and the ninety-per-cent loss figure traces back to one studio co-founder's rough estimate.
So it might not be ninety.
It might not. And the test is narrower than the argument: whether the party setting the price will say what the price is.
[thoughtful] And today, it won't.
Which is the last word. A withheld number is rarely a lie. It's usually just a decision about who gets to do the arithmetic.
[warmly] And sometimes you can do it yourself.
Sometimes, as on page ten, you can do it yourself.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
